title: Non-Unique Factorization in Z[sqrt(-5)]
description: Formalizes the classic counterexample to unique factorization: 6 = 2·3 = (1+√(-5))·(1-√(-5)) in ℤ[√(-5)], with both factorizations into irreducibles. Uses the norm function N(a+b√(-5)) = a²+5b² and its multiplicativity.

overview.historicalContext: The ring Z[sqrt(-5)] is the classical example of a Dedekind domain that is not a UFD, dating back to Kummer's work on ideal numbers in the 1840s.
overview.problemStatement: Show that 6 admits two essentially different factorizations into irreducibles in Z[sqrt(-5)]: 6 = 2*3 = (1+sqrt(-5))*(1-sqrt(-5)).
overview.proofStrategy: Define Z[sqrt(-5)] as pairs (a,b) with norm N(a+b*sqrt(-5)) = a^2+5b^2. Use multiplicativity of the norm to prove irreducibility of factors and show the two factorizations are essentially different by proving 2 does not divide 1+sqrt(-5).
keyInsights: The norm function N(a+b*sqrt(-5)) = a^2+5b^2 is multiplicative and detects units (N(u)=1) and irreducibles
Both 2*3 and (1+sqrt(-5))*(1-sqrt(-5)) equal 6, but 2 does not divide 1+sqrt(-5) in the ring
This provides a concrete, machine-checked counterexample to unique factorization outside Z

conclusion.summary: 193 lines, 17 theorems, 0 axioms, 0 sorries. Proves two distinct factorizations of 6, non-unit status of all factors, and essential difference of the factorizations.
conclusion.implications: Demonstrates that unique factorization fails in Z[sqrt(-5)], motivating the theory of ideal class groups and Dedekind domains.
